Computer Vision is the earliest and biggest success story of deep learning.

Everyday you are interacting with deep learning models: camera filters, video filters, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software, Google image search, and many more.

Deep learning models are the heart of cutting-edge research in autonomous driving, robotics, facial recognition, AI-assisted medical diagnosis, agricultural monitoring, and manufacturing fault detection.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision

Convolutional Neural Networks

  • ConvNet or CNN
  • a type of deep learning architecture / category of neural networks that have proven to be effective in image recognition and classification

Figure 2 (bottom) shows a ConvNet being able to recognize scenes and the system is able to suggest relevant captions.

The LeNet Architecture (1990s)

  • In 1990, computer scientist Yann André LeCun implemented Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in their paper “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition”
  • There have been several new architectures proposed in recent years which are improvements over LeNet

The following operations are basic building blocks of every CNN:

  1. Convolution
  2. Non Linearity
  3. Pooling or Subsampling or Downsampling
  4. Classification
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
LeNet was used to read handwritten digits on bank cheques. The pipeline in the figure (conv, ReLU, pool, repeat, then fully connected) is still the basic shape of most CNNs. The four building blocks listed here are the outline for the rest of the lecture.

Images as Numbers

What does a computer actually see?

Section 1: images as grids of pixel values.

To a computer an image is really a grid of numbers that represent how dark each pixel is.

Hover over a pixel.

This is an 18 × 18 grayscale image of a handwritten “8”. Each square holds one number from 0 (white, no ink) to 255 (black, full ink).

A color image has three such grids stacked together, one each for red, green and blue.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Hover over a few pixels: the edge of a stroke is a middle value, the inside of a stroke is near 255. Click "Show the numbers" to see the whole grid as numbers, which is exactly what the network receives. Note the convention here: higher number means darker (more ink), like MNIST. For photos, higher usually means brighter.

To feed an image into a neural network, we treat the 18×18 pixel image as an array of 324 numbers.

Hover over a pixel or a number: the same value lights up in both places.

When we flatten our image, we lose spatial information that is unique and relevant to the image.

It also makes the neural network very large and computationally expensive.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Hover over a pixel and then over the pixel directly below it. In the grid they are neighbours, but in the flat array they are 18 positions apart. A plain fully connected network has no idea which numbers were next to each other. Size: a 224×224 color photo flattened is 150,528 numbers. One fully connected layer with 1,000 neurons on top of that already needs about 150 million weights. Convolution fixes both problems.

Convolution

Learning image features from small squares of input data

Section 2: the convolution operation, and the three settings that control the size of a feature map.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution

ConvNets derive their names from the “convolution” operator.

The primary purpose of Convolution in a ConvNet is to extract features from the input image to preserve the spatial relationship between pixels by learning image features using small squares of input data.

Consider a 5×5 input image and another 3×3 matrix,

5×5 image
3×3 matrix

Note that for a grayscale image, pixel values range from 0 to 255. The green matrix is a special case where pixel values are only 0 and 1.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Keep the image simple (0s and 1s) so the arithmetic is easy. On the next slide we slide the orange matrix over the green one.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · the convolution operation

Slide the orange matrix, called a “filter” / “kernel” / “feature detector”, over the original matrix by 1 pixel. This movement is called a “stride”.

For every position, we compute:

  • Element-wise multiplication between the two matrices.
  • Add the outputs to get the final integer which forms a single element on the output matrix called a “convolved feature” / “activation map” / “feature map”.

Different values of the filter matrix will produce different feature maps for the same input image.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Press Next to move the filter one position at a time, or Play to animate it. The small red numbers are the filter weights sitting on top of the image. The line under the grids shows the nine multiplications and the sum. Then change the filter with the drop-down and ask: does the same image give the same feature map? (No. Different filters, different feature maps.) Full answer for the default filter: 4 3 4 / 2 4 3 / 2 3 4.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Click through the three positions of the first row on the left. On the right you can step through all nine positions with the explorer. The filter subtracts the right column from the left column. Inside a flat region the two columns are equal, so the answer is 0. Across the edge, left is bright (10) and right is dark (1), so we get a big number. That is how a CNN "sees" a vertical edge.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · different filters, different feature maps

Input
Feature map
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
These are the classic hand-made kernels: identity, two edge (ridge) detectors, sharpen, box blur and Gaussian blur. Click each one. "Slide the filter" animates the kernel sweeping the image and building the feature map row by row. For edge filters the output can be negative: gray means 0, black is negative, white is positive. Key point: in a CNN we do not hand-pick these numbers. The network learns the kernel values during training, and the first layers often end up looking like these edge detectors.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · size of the feature map

The size of the Feature Map or the Convolved Feature is controlled by 3 parameters:

  1. Depth
    • Number of filters for the convolution operation, where each filter detects different patterns or features in the input
    • Essential because it allows a convolutional layer to capture and represent various features and patterns
    • Affects the computational complexity of the network
    • Different filters can specialize in detecting edges, textures, or more complex patterns, ultimately contributing to the network’s ability to understand and classify visual information

Feature map having a depth of 3 (since 3 filters have been used)

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Depth = number of filters. Each filter produces one 2-D feature map; stacking them gives a 3-D output. If a layer has 64 filters, its output has depth 64.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · depth: two filters, two feature maps

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
A 6×6×3 input (an RGB image). Each filter is 3×3×3: it has the same depth as the input. Each filter gives one 4×4 map. Two filters give a 4×4×2 output. Quick check: with 10 filters, what is the output shape? (4×4×10.)

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · stride

  1. Stride
    • Number of pixels by which we slide our filter matrix over the input matrix
      • Stride = 1, move filter 1 pixel at a time
      • Stride = 2, filters move 2 pixels at a time
    • Step size, or how much the filter is moved across (shifts horizontally and vertically) at each step during the convolution operation
    • Larger strides produce smaller feature maps, downsampling the input feature map
      • Stride = 2 will have half the width and half the height of the input feature map
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The explorer starts at stride 2: the filter jumps two pixels, so a 5×5 input gives only a 2×2 output. Switch to stride 1 and compare (3×3). The formula under the grids is the general rule: output = floor((N − F + 2P) / S) + 1, where N is the input size, F the filter size, P the padding and S the stride.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · one input channel

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The animation plays on its own and loops. Use Back / Next to step by hand (this pauses it), Play to resume. The line at the bottom shows the nine multiplications for the current position. Same operation with real-looking numbers, including negatives. Ask students to verify −29: (−8)(0) + 6(3) + 9(−3) + 5(−3) + 5(1) + 7(−2) + 1(−2) + (−5)(0) + 2(3) = 0 + 18 − 27 − 15 + 5 − 14 − 2 + 0 + 6 = −29.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · three input channels

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The animation plays on its own and loops; Back / Next step by hand. With a color image, one filter has one 3×3 slice per input channel. Each slice is convolved with its own channel, the three results are added (−29 + 87 + 14 = 72), then one bias is added (+5) to give 77. So one filter still gives one number per position.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · zero-padding

  1. Zero-padding
    • Used to adjust the spatial dimensions of the input data or feature map before applying convolution
    • Involves adding rows and columns of zeros to the edges of the input matrix (increasing the dimensions of the input)
    • Ensures that the filter remains centered to avoid losing information at the edges
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The explorer starts with padding 1: a ring of zeros (dashed cells) around the 5×5 image. Now the filter can sit centered on the corner pixels and the output stays 5×5, the same size as the input ("same" padding). Switch padding to 0 to see the output shrink to 3×3.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · zero-padding on a color image

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The animation plays on its own and loops; Back / Next step by hand. The "…" cells mean the image continues to the right and below; we only follow the top-left corner. Padding on an RGB image: each channel gets its own ring of zeros and its own kernel slice. 308 + (−498) + 164 = −26, plus bias 1 = −25.

Convolutional Neural Network

Convolution · zero-padding with three input channels

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The same three-channel example as before, now with a border of zeros. The first output is computed with the filter centered on the corner pixel: −5 + (−30) + 24 = −11, plus bias 5 = −6.

Non Linearity

Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and friends

Section 3: activation functions applied to the feature map.

Convolutional Neural Network

Non Linearity

The choice of activation function often depends on the specific problem and testing to determine which one works best for the task at hand.

ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)

  • Computationally cheap to compute f(x) = max(0, x)
  • Less susceptible to vanishing gradient problem
    • Happens when gradients in the network become extremely small, leading to slow convergence or difficulty in training deep networks
    • Two possible gradients:
      • Positive gradient (1): when input is greater than 0, the gradient is a constant 1
      • Zero gradient (0): when the input is less than or equal to 0, the gradient is a constant 0 (making the neuron inactive when the input is negative)
  • Can suffer from the “dying ReLU” problem, where neurons can get stuck in an inactive state during training
    • Leaky ReLU, Parametric ReLU
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Drag the slider through zero and watch the gradient jump from 1 to 0. With plain ReLU a neuron that only ever sees negative inputs gets a gradient of 0 and never updates: that is the dying ReLU problem. Switch to Leaky ReLU: the negative side now has a small slope (α). The demo uses α = 0.1 so the slope is visible; in practice α is often 0.01. Parametric ReLU learns α.

Convolutional Neural Network

Non Linearity · common activation functions

Activation FunctionFormulaOutput RangeProsConsCommon Use
ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)f(x) = max(0, x)[0, ∞)Simple, fast, avoids vanishing gradients, sparse activationDying ReLU (neurons output 0 forever)CNNs, deep networks
Leaky ReLUf(x) = max(αx, x) (α ≈ 0.01)(−∞, ∞)Fixes dying ReLU, allows small gradient for negative valuesStill not zero-centeredCNNs, deep networks
Parametric ReLU (PReLU)f(x) = max(ax, x) (a learned)(−∞, ∞)Learns the negative slopeMore parameters, risk of overfittingAdvanced CNNs
Sigmoidf(x) = 1 / (1 + e−x)(0, 1)Good for binary probabilitiesVanishing gradients, saturates, slowBinary classification output
Tanhf(x) = tanh(x)(−1, 1)Zero-centered, stronger gradients than sigmoidStill saturates, causes vanishing gradientsRNNs, some hidden layers
Softmaxf(xi) = exi / Σj exj(0, 1), sums to 1Converts logits to probabilitiesSensitive to large valuesMulti-class classification output
ELU (Exponential Linear Unit)f(x) = x if x > 0; α(ex − 1) if x ≤ 0(−α, ∞)Smooth, avoids dying ReLU, zero-centeredSlower (uses exponential)Deep CNNs
GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit)f(x) = x Φ(x) (Gaussian CDF Φ)(−∞, ∞)State-of-the-art, smooth, better accuracyComputationally expensiveTransformers (BERT, ViT)
Swishf(x) = x · σ(x)(−∞, ∞)Smooth, often better than ReLUSlightly slowerEfficientNet

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
No need to memorise the whole table. The ones to know: ReLU for hidden layers of CNNs, sigmoid for a binary output, softmax for a multi-class output, and GELU because it shows up in Vision Transformers later today.

Convolutional Neural Network

Non Linearity · ReLU on a feature map

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
ReLU is applied pixel by pixel to the feature map: every negative value (black on the left) becomes 0. Only the positive responses survive. The live demo below the figure does the same thing on the city photo. Pick a filter: the middle image is the raw feature map (gray = 0, black = negative, white = positive); the right image is after ReLU, where all the black (negative) areas become 0. Pooling

Shrinking the feature maps

Section 4: max, average and sum pooling.

Convolutional Neural Network

Pooling

It is common to periodically insert a pooling layer between successive convolutional layers to progressively:

  • reduce the spatial size of the representation
  • reduce the amount of parameters (computational complexity) of the network
  • make the network invariant to small transformations, distortions, and translations in the input image (since we take the maximum / average value in a local neighborhood)

Types of pooling include: max, average, sum

2×2 filters, stride 2
Rectified feature map (single depth slice)
→
Max pool
Hover over an output cell.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Hover over each output cell: it is the max of its colored 2×2 block, e.g. max(1, 1, 5, 6) = 6. Switch to Average and Sum. Pooling has no weights to learn. Each depth slice is pooled on its own, so the depth stays the same (224×224×64 becomes 112×112×64). Invariance: if the 6 moves one pixel inside its block, the max does not change.

Convolutional Neural Network

Pooling · max vs. sum on a feature map

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Both outputs are half the width and height. Max keeps the strongest response in each block. Sum adds them, so busy regions get brighter. Live demo: the left image is a rectified feature map of the city photo. Click "Pool 2×" or "3×" to stack pooling layers: each one halves the size again (198×131 → 99×65 → 49×32 → 24×16). The buildings are still recognisable after several poolings, which is why pooling barely hurts classification while cutting computation a lot.

Convolutional Neural Network

Pooling · putting the blocks together

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The same pipeline as the LeNet figure (conv + ReLU, pool, conv + ReLU, pool, fully connected, fully connected, output), but every feature map here is really computed in the browser from the giraffe photo. The animation steps through the network one block at a time; the box at the bottom says what happens and gives the shape after each block. Hover over a stage to jump to it, or use Back / Next. Point out the shapes: width and height go down (112 → 56 → 28), the number of maps stays 4 here (real networks increase it, e.g. VGG 64 → 128 → 256 → 512). Be clear that the filters here are hand-picked edge detectors and the class scores are made up for illustration. A trained network learns its filters and its scores.

Convolutional Neural Network

Classification · flatten, then fully connected

Flatten Layer converts a three-dimensional layer in the network into a one-dimensional vector to fit the input of a fully-connected layer for classification.

  • No weights to learn: it only reshapes.
  • Size = height × width × depth. In LeNet-5: 5 × 5 × 16 = 400 values.

Fully Connected Layer is a Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) that uses an activation function in the output layer.

  • Every input connects to every neuron: z = W·x + b, then an activation.
  • Hidden dense layers usually use ReLU.
  • The output layer has one neuron per class; softmax turns its scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
  • Most of a classic CNN’s parameters live here. VGG-16’s first dense layer alone has 7 × 7 × 512 × 4096 ≈ 103 million weights.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The animation: three 3×3 feature maps (depth 3, one color per map) are flattened into one column of 27 numbers. Notice the colors interleave: Keras flattens "channels last", so it takes all 3 channels of pixel 1, then all 3 of pixel 2, and so on. Then every number connects to every neuron of a dense layer, and finally the 3 output neurons give scores that softmax turns into probabilities. Flattening is fine here: by this point the convolution and pooling layers have already turned the image into a compact set of features, so we are no longer throwing away raw spatial layout. Hover over an output to see its score and probability. Back / Next step through by hand.

Convolutional Neural Network

Classification · choosing the last layer

Choosing the right last-layer activation and loss function for your model · click a row

Problem typeLast-layer activationLoss functionExample
Binary classificationsigmoidbinary_crossentropycat or not cat
Multiclass, single-label classificationsoftmaxcategorical_crossentropywhich digit, 0–9
Multiclass, multilabel classificationsigmoidbinary_crossentropywhich objects are in the photo
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Click each row of the table. Drag the sliders to change the raw scores (logits) coming out of the last layer: - Binary: one output neuron, sigmoid squashes it to a probability. Above 0.5 means "cat". - Multiclass single-label: softmax makes the classes compete. The probabilities always add up to 1 and we pick the highest. - Multilabel: one sigmoid per class, each is independent. They do not add up to 1, and several labels can be "on" at once. The loss line shows cross-entropy for the true label marked with a check: it is −log(probability of the right answer), so it is small when the model is confident and right, and large when it is confident and wrong. The Keras code updates with the row you pick.

CNN Architectures

AlexNet, VGGNet and ResNet

Section 5: three landmark CNNs from the ImageNet era.

Convolutional Neural Network

CNN Architectures: AlexNet (2012)

AlexNet, which employed an 8-layer CNN, won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge 2012 by a large margin (Russakovsky et al., 2013). It consists of 8 layers: 5 convolutional layers, 2 fully connected hidden layers and 1 fully connected output layer. AlexNet used the ReLU instead of the sigmoid as its activation function.

15.3%top-5 error, vs. 26.2% for the runner-up
ReLUtrained about 6× faster than tanh
Dropout0.5 in fc6 and fc7 against overfitting
Augmentationrandom crops and flips of 1.2M images
2 GPUsabout 6 days of training
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
AlexNet is the moment deep learning took over computer vision. Compared with LeNet: much bigger, much deeper, ReLU instead of sigmoid, trained on GPUs, and dropout in the fully connected layers. The layer explorer steps through the network (or hover a layer). For each layer it shows the filter size, the output shape (with the size formula), and the number of parameters. Point at the bar chart: the three fully connected layers hold about 94% of the 62 million parameters; fc6 alone has 37.7 million. The convolutions do most of the computation but have few weights. This is why later networks (GoogLeNet, ResNet) replaced the big dense layers with global average pooling. Shapes use the common 227×227 input (the paper says 224, which does not divide evenly).

Convolutional Neural Network

CNN Architectures: VGGNet (2014)

In VGGNet architecture:

  • The first block has 64 filters in each of its convolutional layers.
  • The second block doubles the filter depth to 128 filters in its convolutional layers.
  • Subsequent blocks further double this number to 256, then 512, maintaining a doubling pattern.

This gradual increase in the number of filters while maintaining a small 3×3 kernel size allows VGGNet to capture increasingly complex features at each depth level, balancing computational cost and performance.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
The animation walks through VGG-16 block by block (hover a block to jump to it). Each slab is the output of a block: its height is the width/height of the feature map, its thickness is the number of channels. The pattern: every time max-pooling halves the width and height, the number of filters doubles. Spatial size goes down (224 → 112 → 56 → 28 → 14 → 7), depth goes up (64 → 128 → 256 → 512). The amount of data per layer drops from 3.2 million numbers in block 1 to 25,088 after the last pool, which is what gets flattened into the fully connected layers.

Convolutional Neural Network

CNN Architectures: VGGNet (2014)

VGGNet most commonly comes in two main depth variants:

  • VGG-16: 16 weight layers total, consisting of 13 convolutional layers and 3 fully connected layers.
  • VGG-19: 19 weight layers total, consisting of 16 convolutional layers and 3 fully connected layers.

These contain

  • convolutional layers that primarily use:
    • 3×3 filters with stride 1 and padding 1,
    • arranged in blocks with max-pooling layers (2×2 filters, stride 2) between blocks to reduce spatial dimensions
  • fully connected layers, including two layers with 4096 units each
  • a final classification layer with 1000 units for ImageNet classes.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Top right: switch between VGG-16 and VGG-19. The only difference is one extra 3×3 conv layer in blocks 3, 4 and 5 (2-2-3-3-3 vs 2-2-4-4-4). Parameters: about 138 million vs 144 million, most of them in the fully connected layers. Bottom right, why only 3×3? Step through 1, 2 and 3 stacked layers: the center output pixel "sees" a 3×3, then 5×5, then 7×7 patch of the input. So three 3×3 layers see as much as one 7×7 layer, but with 27C² weights instead of 49C² (45% fewer), and with three ReLUs instead of one, so more non-linearity. Connect to earlier slides: 3×3 filters with stride 1 and padding 1 keep the width and height the same ((N − 3 + 2)/1 + 1 = N). Only the 2×2, stride 2 max-pooling shrinks the image.

Convolutional Neural Network

CNN Architectures: ResNet (2015)

ResNet architecture is designed around residual blocks that enable very deep networks by using shortcut or “skip” connections to add the input of a block directly to its output.

  • The layers learn only the residual F(x), the change to make; the block outputs F(x) + x.
  • If a block is not needed, it can learn F(x) ≈ 0 and simply pass x through.
  • Gradients flow straight back through the shortcut, so even 152-layer networks still train.
  • Deep versions (below) use a bottleneck block: 1×1 → 3×3 → 1×1.
  • ResNet-152 won ILSVRC 2015 with 3.57% top-5 error.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Right: the residual block, animated. The signal x splits: one copy goes through the two weight layers (F(x)), the other takes the shortcut, and they are added. Turn the skip connection off to get a "plain" block. The bars below show how strong the gradient is at each of 20 layers during backpropagation (layer 20 is next to the loss). Without skips the gradient shrinks a little at every layer and the early layers barely learn: the vanishing gradient. With skips the shortcut carries the gradient back almost unchanged. These bars are illustrative, not measured. Bottom: the full ResNet-50 layout (bottleneck blocks in 4 stages, 64 → 512 channels, then average pooling and a 1000-way output).

Convolutional Neural Network

A one-slide summary of the three architectures. The trend: deeper networks, smaller filters, and (with ResNet) a trick that makes very deep networks trainable.

Beyond CNNs

Vision Transformers and Generative Adversarial Networks

Section 6: two other families of vision models.

Vision Transformers (ViT)

Each flattened patch vector is multiplied by a learnable projection matrix that produces a vector of size D:

Patch embedding = W · Flattened patch + b

ViTs split an image into small, fixed-size patches. Suppose you have an image of size 224×224×3 (height × width × channels).

Patch size

Hover over the photo to pick a patch.

Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
With patch size 16: 224/16 = 14 patches per side, 14 × 14 = 196 patches. Each patch is 16×16×3 = 768 numbers, flattened into a vector [x1, x2, ..., x768] to turn 2-D spatial information into a linear sequence. So the Transformer sees the image as a "sentence" of 196 "words". Try patch size 8: four times as many tokens (784), and attention cost grows with the square of the number of tokens. This is why ViTs usually use 16 or 14.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)

Two neural networks work in opposition: one generates data, while the other evaluates whether the data is real or generated.

  • Generator (G) creates fake data from random noise and tries to fool the discriminator into thinking fake data is real
  • Discriminator (D) receives real and fake data and learns to distinguish real from fake
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Left: the structure of a GAN (same as the PDF figure), animated. Gray dots are random noise going into the generator; they come out as fake images. Green dots are real images. Both go to the discriminator. Then the two losses update the networks in turn: the discriminator learns to tell them apart, the generator learns to fool it. Right: a simulation of training. Press Play or drag the slider. - Sample images: what the generator produces at that point. Pure noise at the start, blurry blobs, then clean digits. - The plot: green dots are real data, orange dots are generated data. At the start the fakes are a blob in the middle; during training they spread out to cover the real clusters. - The background shows the best possible discriminator, D(x) = p_real / (p_real + p_fake): green where it says "real", orange where it says "fake". When the fakes match the real data, it can only say 0.5 everywhere (gray) and the meters both go to 0.5. This is a simulation for teaching (no network is trained in the browser), but the end state, D = 0.5, is exactly the theoretical goal of GAN training. A forger (generator) and a detective (discriminator): as the detective gets better, the forger is forced to get better too. At the end we keep the generator.

Main Tasks and Applications

Classification, detection and segmentation

Section 7: what we use these models for.

Convolutional Neural Network

Main Tasks and Applications

Image Classification

  • one label for the whole image

Object Detection

  • Classification + localization “what is the main object and where is it?”
    • One class label, one bounding box
    • One dominant object
  • Object Detection “what objects are present and where is each one?”
    • A set of bounding boxes and confidence scores for each box
    • Handles multiple objects and multiple classes in the same image

The viewer cycles through the three tasks on the same photo; click a tab to stop on one. The panel on the right is what the model actually outputs for each task: one label, one label plus one box, or a list of boxes each with a class and a confidence score. Hover over a box to highlight it. (Scores are illustrative.) In the PDF figure: read left to right, each task gives more detail than the one before. Classification says "cat". Localization adds one box. Detection finds every object with its own box. Segmentation (next slide) goes down to individual pixels.

Convolutional Neural Network

Main Tasks and Applications

Image Segmentation

  • Semantic Segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel in the image
    • Groups all objects of the same class into a single combined region
  • Instance Segmentation separates each individual object instance in an image within the same class
    • Assigns unique identifiers to each object instance so that overlapping or adjacent objects are distinctly segmented
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Hover over the photo: the zoom box shows the label of every pixel around the cursor, which is literally what a segmentation model outputs (one label per pixel). Switch between Semantic and Instance: semantic gives both giraffes the same label (1 = giraffe), instance gives them different ids (1 and 2). The slider fades the mask in and out. PDF figure: semantic segmentation paints all three dogs one color ("dog"). Instance segmentation gives each dog its own color (Dog 1, Dog 2, Dog 3). Applications: self-driving cars (road, pedestrians), medical imaging (tumour boundaries), satellite and farm images (field boundaries).

Notice how many of these are transformer-based (ViT, Swin, DETR, SegFormer) while modern CNNs (ConvNeXt, EfficientNetV2) are still very competitive. The building blocks from today (convolution, pooling, skip connections, patches) show up in nearly all of them.

Discussion

Despite progress, several challenges remain..

What do you think are the remaining challenges in Deep Computer Vision?

  1. Data and labels. Models need huge labelled datasets; pixel-level labels for segmentation are slow and expensive to make.
  2. Robustness. Small changes in lighting, weather, camera or a few adversarial pixels can fool a model that is very accurate on test data.
  3. Bias and fairness. Models can work worse for groups under-represented in the training data, for example in face recognition.
  4. Interpretability. It is hard to explain why a model made a decision, which matters in medicine and driving.
  5. Compute and deployment. Large models are expensive to train and too heavy for phones, drones and other edge devices.
Jennifer Joyce M. Montemayor / CSC173 / Deep Learning for Computer Vision
Let students answer first, then click to reveal possible answers one at a time. Other good answers: rare objects (the long tail), video and 3-D understanding, privacy and surveillance concerns, and common-sense reasoning about scenes.
